sentences.show: He fought for Japan, then for the Soviet Union, then for Nazi Germany. And the Americans captured him on D-Day.
At least, that's the legend of Yang Kyoungjong.
The story goes like this. A young Korean is drafted into the Japanese army. Korea was a Japanese colony.
In 1939, on the Mongolian border, the Soviets capture him, and send him to a labour camp.
Then Hitler invades Russia. The Red Army needs men, so they hand him a rifle.
In 1943, near Kharkov, the Germans capture him.
And they put him in a German uniform, with a battalion of former Soviet prisoners.
They send him to France, to guard the coast of Normandy.
American paratroopers capture Asian men in German uniforms. No one can understand a word they say.
And then there's this photo. A prisoner in Normandy. The Army caption calls him a "young Japanese".
Famous historians have told Yang's story as fact. But none of them gave a source.
A Korean documentary found no proof he ever existed. One historian thinks the man in the photo was from Georgia.
But an American officer did report capturing four Koreans in German uniforms, who had fought for Japan and Russia first.
So was Yang Kyoungjong real? Or did the war invent him?
Real man or legend? Tell us below, and subscribe for the next one.
